entry.title: Tidewatch 2.0 is out
entry.content:
Tidewatch 2.0 predicts a full year of tides in under a second, about ten times faster than 1.x. Setup is now one command, and the new guide walks a harbour office through its first table.

What changed

  • A new prediction engine, rewritten in Rust.
  • One install command for every platform.
  • Clear error messages when survey data is missing.

Thank you to the forty contributors who made this release.
entry.summary: Faster predictions, a simpler setup and a new guide for harbour offices.

entry.title: The harbour at low tide, as a dataset

link.title: The harbour at low tide, as a dataset

entry.content:
Twice a day the water leaves and the harbour shows its bones. For a year I logged every low tide with a cheap sensor on the second mooring post.

The readings disagreed with my own predictions by up to eleven minutes. The fault was mine: a rounding error that had lived in the code for three years. The fix was one line; finding it took a winter.
entry.summary: What a year of low-water measurements taught me about the harbour, and about my own code.

entry.title: Keeping a commonplace book in plain text

link.title: Keeping a commonplace book in plain text

entry.content:
A commonplace book is a notebook of things worth keeping: commands, error messages, quotations, the name of a bolt. I have kept mine in plain text files for twelve years.1 This is how it works.

The rules

  1. Write the date before anything else.
  2. Copy the source with every note, even a page number.
  3. Never delete an entry; cross it out instead.

Files - one text file per month, named by date.

Index - a list of subjects at the top of each file.

A worked example

Subject Files Notes
Tides 2024-03, 2025-01 survey formats
Rust 2025-06 borrow checker notes
Bread 2023-11 a recipe from a neighbour

Write it down the first time, or look it up forever.

When the notes moved to a computer I wrote a tiny script to rebuild the index:

import pathlib, re

index = {}
for note in sorted(pathlib.Path("notes").glob("*.txt")):
    for subject in re.findall(r"^# (.+)$", note.read_text(), re.M):
        index.setdefault(subject, []).append(note.stem)
print(index)

  1. Before that, a paper notebook that I still keep for sketches. ↩
entry.summary: How I keep twelve years of notes in plain text files, with the small script that indexes them.

entry.title: A tiny cache for slow harbour Wi-Fi

link.title: A tiny cache for slow harbour Wi-Fi

entry.content: The ferry terminal has one Wi-Fi access point and four hundred passengers. I added a small offline cache to the timetable page so it keeps working when the connection drops. It took forty lines and saved a lot of shouting at the ticket desk.
entry.summary: The ferry terminal's Wi-Fi drops every few minutes, so the timetable page now works offline.

entry.title: Five years of maintaining an open-source library

link.title: Five years of maintaining an open-source library

entry.content:
Tidewatch turned five this spring. Here is what I learned, in the order I learned it.

  1. Say no to features early, kindly and in writing.
  2. Write the guide before the code.
  3. Take holidays. The library will survive.
entry.summary: What I would tell myself on day one: say no early, write the docs first, and take holidays.

entry.title: Why I still write tests first

link.title: Why I still write tests first

entry.content: Writing the test first makes me decide what the code should do before I decide how. It is slower on Monday and much faster by Friday.
entry.summary: A short note on the habit that has saved me the most time.

entry.title: Porting the tide math to Rust

link.title: Porting the tide math to Rust

entry.content: The new core is ten times faster, but the old Python version stays as the reference. Every release checks that both give the same answers for a thousand harbours.
entry.summary: Notes from rewriting the prediction core, and why the old version stays.
